name: Kira Young

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making the time, Kira. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We have no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government, and we don't sell anything. Everything you tell me stays confidential, so you can say what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm the office administrator at a small architecture practice, seven of us above a bakery on the high street. I do the diary for the two partners, chase invoices, book site visits, keep the drawing register up to date and order everything from printer toner to biscuits. I use an AI assistant for most of my first drafts, meeting notes and so on, and then I fix what it gets wrong. I'm still learning the planning paperwork, which is a whole language of its own.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like that nobody really owns the office systems, so I get to build them. Last month I set up an automatic reminder for site visits and Gareth, one of the partners, actually said thank you. What wears me out is the pay: I share a flat with my friend Priya, and after rent I've got less than a month's money in the bank, always.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. I'll read it as written. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say what I already say: it's a decent tool, not magic. I'd probably post a bit of a told-you-so, because I've seen it make up planning reference numbers with total confidence. At work I'd keep pushing to use it for the boring stuff.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means I stay useful, which is good. I'm the person in the office who knows how to get the tools to work, so a world where they're only half good keeps me needed. The trouble is that being needed doesn't come with better pay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep building little systems at work and write them up, so I can show the partners what I've saved them. Then I'd ask for a raise with numbers attached, maybe in the spring review. I'd also carry on helping the food bank with its volunteer rota on Saturdays, which might turn into a paid side thing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit flat, honestly, but fine. The job's safe, the money's the problem.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You use AI every day already. Does the plateau feel like a letdown to you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Kind of, yes. I was half hoping for something that shakes up who gets paid what. I've saved the partners hours every week with free AI tools, and my pay hasn't moved a penny.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With less than a month saved, what does a normal bad month look like for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The boiler goes, or Priya's between jobs and I cover more of the rent. Then I'm on the overdraft until payday. It's not dramatic, it's just always there.

say: I'd say AI is a **decent tool**, not magic, and post a small told-you-so.
At work I'd keep pushing to use it for the **boring stuff**.
think: Privately, a half-good AI **keeps me needed** as the office's tool person.
Being needed still doesn't bring **better pay**, which is the real problem.
do: Write up the **hours saved** by my office systems for the partners.
Ask for a **raise** with those numbers at the spring review.
Keep running the **food bank rota**, which might turn into paid work.
feel: **A bit flat**, with the job safe but money always tight.
S0.quote: I've saved the partners hours every week with free AI tools, and my pay hasn't moved a penny.
fieldNote: Kira already uses AI daily and sees the plateau as **confirmation**, not relief.
Her frustration is about **who gets the gains**, a clear progressive thread.
The **overdraft** is a constant background pressure, not a crisis.

steps.text: Write up hours saved by my office systems for the partners
Ask for a raise at the spring review with figures
Turn the food bank volunteer rota into paid side work

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's happening and we should shape it, not just let it happen to us. Online I'd say the time saved should go to the staff as shorter weeks or more pay, not just bigger profit. At work I'd offer to lead the switch-over.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, a lot of my job goes. Diary, invoices, orders, booking: that's the card, word for word. My hope is that I'm the one who runs the tools rather than the one they replace, but I'm junior and that's a coin toss.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd spend evenings on a short online course in office automation, the kind with a certificate. I'd start charging small charities for setting up their booking and rota systems, maybe fifty pounds a job. And I'd tell the partners I want a new title, something like operations coordinator, before someone else gets the idea.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Excited and sick at the same time, if that makes sense.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at the practice would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sunita, our bookkeeper, honestly. She's brilliant, but she's in her fifties and doesn't trust any of it. If the accounts software does the reconciling, the partners will look at her salary first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the partners should share the savings. How would you actually ask?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask for a four-day week once the savings show up, and I'd bring the numbers. If AI saves our practice ten hours a week, I want a day of that back, not a pat on the head. I don't think they'd say yes the first time.

say: I'd say we should **shape the change**, not let it happen to us.
Online I'd argue saved time should go to staff as **shorter weeks** or pay.
think: Privately a lot of **my job goes**, since the card lists it word for word.
Whether I **run the tools** or get replaced by them is a coin toss.
do: Take an evening **office automation course** with a certificate.
Charge small charities about **fifty pounds** to set up booking systems.
Ask the partners for an **operations coordinator** title.
feel: **Excited and sick** at the same time.
S1.quote: If AI saves our practice ten hours a week, I want a day of that back, not a pat on the head.
fieldNote: Kira moves **first**, aiming to own the tools before they own her job.
Her progressive views show in the **four-day week** ask.
She worries for **Sunita**, the older bookkeeper, more than for herself.
She admits being junior makes her survival a **coin toss**.

steps.text: Finish an evening office automation course with a certificate
Set up booking systems for small charities at fifty pounds a job
Ask the partners for a new operations coordinator title
Push for a four-day week once savings show

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this needs a political answer now, not in 2028: a basic income, or at least a proper safety net. I'd probably be loud about it online. At work I'd say, calmly, that we all need a plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think the practice shrinks to the partners and an AI. Maybe even the partners shrink. My job is all thinking work on a screen, so it's gone on day one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd try to make myself the person who sets up AI for other small firms, quickly, while it's still new and confusing. I'd move back in with my mum if I had to, to cut rent. And I'd join whatever campaign was pushing for income support.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. My stomach drops a bit just saying it out loud.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You use the tools every day. Does that give you a head start here, or not?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For about six months, maybe. Being early helps until the tools don't need anyone to set them up. Knowing the AI tools well only buys me a head start in a race that finishes in 2028.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The card says robots come about three years after the thinking AI. Does that gap mean anything for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not really for me, because nothing in my job is hands-on. It means the builders on our sites carry on a bit longer. I'd joke about learning to lay bricks, but it's half a joke.

say: I'd say we need a **political answer** now, like a basic income.
At work I'd calmly say we all need **a plan**.
think: Privately the practice **shrinks** to the partners and an AI.
My job is all **screen work**, so it goes on day one.
do: Sell **AI setup** help to other small firms while it's new.
Move back in with **my mum** if rent becomes impossible.
feel: **Alarmed**, with a drop in the stomach saying it aloud.
S2.quote: Knowing the AI tools well only buys me a head start in a race that finishes in 2028.
fieldNote: Even the most AI-ready junior sees her **early start** as worth months, not years.
She sees no benefit from the **robot delay**, as her work is all thinking.
Her fallback is **family**: moving back in with her mum.

steps.text: Offer paid AI setup help to small local firms
Move back in with my mum if rent gets impossible
Join a campaign for basic income support

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got a few years, so use them: rules on how companies cut staff, and free retraining. Online I'd be the annoying one sharing how-to guides. At work I'd keep leading on the tools.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think I'd have time to turn my side work into something real. Five years is enough to build a small business setting up systems for charities and small shops. Whether it survives AGI itself, I honestly don't know.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In year one I'd register as self-employed and get five or six regular clients. I'd save every bit of side money, aiming for three months of rent. I'd also stay at the practice part-time if they'd let me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but in a busy way. Having something to do with my hands, so to speak, helps.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Five years. What would you do in year one that you couldn't in the fast one?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For a while. Holt and Ferris (the architecture practice I work for) won't need an office administrator by 2031, so I'd rather leave on my own terms.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you still stay at the architecture practice?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably until about 2029. By then I'd want the business paying my share of the rent, or I'd be looking at something completely different.

say: I'd call for **rules on job cuts** and free retraining.
Online I'd share **how-to guides** for people catching up.
think: Privately five years is enough to build a **small business**.
I honestly **don't know** if that business survives AGI itself.
do: Register as **self-employed** and win five or six regular clients.
Save all side money toward **three months** of rent.
Ask the practice to keep me on **part-time**.
feel: **Anxious but busy**, which feels better than sitting still.
S3.quote: Holt and Ferris (the architecture practice I work for) won't need an office administrator by 2031, so I'd rather leave on my own terms.
fieldNote: Kira treats five years as **runway** for a small business.
She's honest that the business might **not survive** AGI either.
She plans to **leave early** on her own terms rather than wait.

steps.text: Register as self-employed and sign five or six clients
Save side money toward three months of rent

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fifth and last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough time if we start now, and that waiting is how people get left behind. I'd push for a shorter working week as AI makes everyone more productive. I'd sound almost hopeful.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think I could genuinely do well in the first half of that decade. The second half, I don't know. Even with ten years, everything I'm good at is thinking work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd study part-time for something with people at the centre, maybe social work, which mixes judgment with home visits. I'd keep my side business going as the income. And I'd actually start a pension, which I've been putting off.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried, still. But I can breathe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Ten years. Is there a career you'd pick that you wouldn't pick with two?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe. I've always liked the bit of my job where I calm down a stressed client. With ten years I'd train for work where a person sits in someone's kitchen and listens.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Priya, your flatmate, about this one?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell Priya (my flatmate) to learn the tools now, because she's a receptionist at a dental surgery and that's the same boat. She'd roll her eyes and then ask me to show her.

say: I'd say **ten years** is enough if we start now.
I'd push for a **shorter working week** as productivity rises.
think: Privately I could do well in the **first half** of that decade.
Everything I'm good at is still **thinking work**, so the second half worries me.
do: Study **social work** part-time, mixing judgment with home visits.
Keep the **side business** running as income.
S4.quote: With ten years I'd train for work where a person sits in someone's kitchen and listens.
fieldNote: The decade lets Kira consider a **people-centred** career she'd skip under pressure.
She still sees her own skills as **thinking work**, so the end point worries her.
She plans to **teach Priya** the tools, showing her helper instinct.

steps.text: Study social work part-time at the college
Keep the charity systems business running as income
Open a pension and pay in monthly

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028. I'm the one who's supposed to be ready, and I'd still only get a few months out of it. What would help is a proper income floor, so people like me can retrain without the overdraft.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask who gets the money the tools save. Every hour I've saved with AI went to the partners' profit, and nobody asked the person who saved it.

headlineQuote: Every hour I've saved with AI went to the partners' profit, and nobody asked the person who saved it.
portrait: Kira is a **27-year-old** junior administrator at a seven-person architecture practice.
She uses **AI tools daily** and builds the office's systems.
She shares a flat and lives close to her **overdraft** every month.
Her progressive views focus on **who gets the gains** from AI.
She's uneasy in the plateau and **alarmed** only when AGI arrives in two years.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, since even her early start would last only months.
whatWouldHelp: An **income floor** so she can retrain without living on the overdraft.
